courses.title: Clinical Biochemistry and Enzymology
courses.description: Clinical enzymology, isoenzymes, biochemical markers of organ damage, inborn errors of metabolism, and free radicals and antioxidants.

topics.title: Principles of Clinical Enzymology
topics.summary: Why enzymes appear in plasma, factors affecting measurement, and units of activity.

material.heading: Plasma enzymes
material.body: Most enzymes measured clinically are intracellular and leak into plasma when cells are damaged or proliferate; plasma-specific enzymes (e.g. clotting factors, lipoprotein lipase, pseudocholinesterase) are secreted into plasma to act there, and a fall may indicate reduced synthesis (e.g. low cholinesterase in liver disease). The plasma level depends on the rate of release (extent of damage, intracellular concentration, cell location — cytoplasmic enzymes like ALT rise with milder damage than mitochondrial ones), and the rate of clearance (half-life). Enzyme activity is expressed in international units (U/L — µmol of substrate converted per minute) or katals (mol/s) under defined conditions of temperature, pH and substrate concentration (zero-order kinetics, [S] ≫ Km).

material.heading: Pre-analytical factors
material.body: Haemolysis falsely raises enzymes present in red cells (LDH, AST, acid phosphatase). Strenuous exercise, intramuscular injections and trauma raise CK. EDTA and citrate chelate metal cofactors (e.g. inhibit ALP, which needs Zn2+ and Mg2+), so serum or heparin plasma is used for most enzymes. Storage temperature and delays affect labile enzymes. Physiological variations: ALP is higher in growing children (bone) and pregnancy (placental ALP); CK is higher in muscular individuals and people of African ancestry. Reference intervals must therefore be population-appropriate.

topics.title: Isoenzymes and Organ-specific Markers
topics.summary: LDH, CK and ALP isoenzymes, and enzyme patterns in liver, muscle, bone and pancreatic disease.

material.heading: Isoenzymes
material.body: Isoenzymes catalyse the same reaction but differ in structure, tissue distribution and properties, allowing tissue localisation. Creatine kinase: CK-MM (skeletal muscle), CK-MB (myocardium — 20–30% of cardiac CK) and CK-BB (brain). Lactate dehydrogenase is a tetramer of H and M subunits: LD1 (H4, heart and red cells) to LD5 (M4, liver and skeletal muscle); an 'LD1/LD2 flip' (LD1 > LD2) historically suggested myocardial infarction or haemolysis. Alkaline phosphatase isoenzymes: liver, bone, placental (heat-stable — survives 65 °C) and intestinal; they are separated by electrophoresis or heat inactivation (bone ALP is most heat-labile: 'bone burns').
keyPoints: CK-MM muscle; CK-MB heart; CK-BB brain
Placental ALP heat-stable; bone ALP heat-labile

material.heading: Patterns
material.body: Liver: hepatocellular damage raises ALT and AST (ALT more specific); cholestasis raises ALP and GGT (GGT confirms hepatic origin and rises with alcohol and enzyme-inducing drugs). Muscle: very high CK in rhabdomyolysis (risk of myoglobinuric AKI), muscular dystrophy (Duchenne — CK massively raised from birth), myositis and statin myopathy. Heart: troponins have replaced enzymes as preferred markers. Pancreas: amylase and lipase in acute pancreatitis (lipase more specific). Bone: ALP in Paget's disease, osteomalacia/rickets, bone metastases, healing fractures; acid phosphatase and PSA historically for prostate cancer. G6PD and pyruvate kinase are red-cell enzymes measured to diagnose haemolytic anaemias.
keyPoints: GGT confirms hepatic ALP; ↑ with alcohol

topics.title: Inborn Errors of Metabolism
topics.summary: Principles, presentation, newborn screening and examples of amino acid, carbohydrate and storage disorders.

material.heading: Principles
material.body: Inborn errors of metabolism are mostly autosomal recessive single-gene defects of enzymes or transporters, causing accumulation of substrate proximal to the block, deficiency of the product, or diversion to alternative pathways (Garrod's concept). Presentation in neonates may mimic sepsis: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, coma, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, jaundice, unusual odours (musty — PKU; maple syrup — MSUD; sweaty feet — isovaleric acidaemia). Investigations: blood glucose, gases, ammonia, lactate, urine organic acids, plasma amino acids, tandem mass spectrometry. Newborn screening (heel-prick blood spot) detects treatable conditions such as PKU, congenital hypothyroidism and sickle cell disease.

material.heading: Examples
material.body: Amino acids: phenylketonuria (phenylalanine hydroxylase; low-phenylalanine diet), maple syrup urine disease (branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase), homocystinuria (cystathionine β-synthase — lens dislocation downwards, thrombosis, marfanoid habitus), alkaptonuria, albinism. Carbohydrates: galactosaemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase — jaundice, vomiting, cataracts, E. coli sepsis after milk feeding; remove galactose/lactose), hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B — hypoglycaemia after fruit/sucrose), glycogen storage diseases (von Gierke — glucose-6-phosphatase; Pompe — acid maltase, cardiomyopathy; McArdle — muscle phosphorylase, exercise cramps). Lysosomal storage disorders: Gaucher (glucocerebrosidase — hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises), Tay–Sachs (hexosaminidase A — cherry-red spot), Niemann–Pick, mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler, Hunter — X-linked).

topics.title: Free Radicals, Antioxidants and Oxidative Stress
topics.summary: Reactive oxygen species, antioxidant defences, oxidative damage in disease, and assessment.

material.heading: Free radicals
material.body: Free radicals are molecules with unpaired electrons. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) include superoxide (O2•−), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, not a radical but a precursor) and the highly reactive hydroxyl radical (•OH, formed via the Fenton reaction with Fe2+). Reactive nitrogen species include nitric oxide and peroxynitrite. Sources: mitochondrial electron transport leakage, NADPH oxidase in phagocytes (the respiratory burst — deficient in chronic granulomatous disease), xanthine oxidase in reperfusion injury, cytochrome P450, radiation, smoking and pollutants. ROS damage lipids (lipid peroxidation — measured as malondialdehyde, MDA), proteins and DNA (8-oxo-deoxyguanosine).

material.heading: Antioxidants and disease
material.body: Enzymatic antioxidants: superoxide dismutase (O2•− → H2O2; Cu/Zn and Mn forms), catalase (H2O2 → H2O + O2) and glutathione peroxidase (selenium-dependent; uses reduced glutathione, regenerated by glutathione reductase with NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway — hence haemolysis in G6PD deficiency). Non-enzymatic antioxidants: vitamin E (α-tocopherol, lipid-soluble, protects membranes), vitamin C (water-soluble, regenerates vitamin E), β-carotene, glutathione, uric acid, bilirubin, and dietary polyphenols (e.g. in fruits, vegetables, tea, and Nigerian plants such as bitter kola). Oxidative stress (imbalance favouring oxidants) is implicated in atherosclerosis, diabetes complications, ischaemia–reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cancer, ageing, sickle cell disease, malaria and paracetamol toxicity (NAPQI depletes glutathione).
keyPoints: Vitamin E: membranes; vitamin C: aqueous
Oxidative stress in atherosclerosis, diabetes, SCD

topics.title: Clinical Biochemistry of Nutrition and Toxicology
topics.summary: Assessing nutritional status biochemically, trace elements, and common poisonings.

material.heading: Nutritional biochemistry
material.body: Biochemical markers of nutritional status: albumin (half-life ~20 days; also falls in inflammation, liver and renal disease), transthyretin/prealbumin (half-life ~2 days, reflects recent intake), transferrin, total lymphocyte count, nitrogen balance, and specific micronutrients (serum ferritin for iron; serum retinol for vitamin A; 25-hydroxyvitamin D for vitamin D status; serum B12 and red cell folate; serum zinc — lowered by inflammation; urinary iodine for population iodine status). Refeeding syndrome in malnourished patients: hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and thiamine deficiency — monitor and replace. Obesity-related biochemistry includes insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia and raised liver enzymes (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease).
keyPoints: 25-OH vitamin D for vitamin D status

material.heading: Toxicology
material.body: Biochemistry supports diagnosis and management of poisoning. Paracetamol: plasma level plotted against time since ingestion on a treatment nomogram (from 4 hours) guides N-acetylcysteine; check LFTs, INR and creatinine. Salicylates: mixed acid–base disturbance; urinary alkalinisation; haemodialysis for severe cases. Organophosphates (common in Nigeria from agricultural pesticides): reduced red cell and plasma cholinesterase. Lead: raised blood lead, basophilic stippling, raised zinc protoporphyrin; chelation with EDTA/succimer. Methanol and ethylene glycol: raised osmolal gap then raised anion gap acidosis; treat with fomepizole or ethanol and dialysis. Carbon monoxide: raised carboxyhaemoglobin (co-oximetry); treat with high-flow oxygen. Kerosene ingestion (common in children): aspiration pneumonitis — do not induce vomiting.
keyPoints: Toxic alcohols: osmolal then anion gap
